summary: Documents how BGP-4 met the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard, reporting experience with the protocol. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A report of how well a routing protocol has worked in real life.

questions: how did bgp-4 reach draft standard
subtitle: A field report on how BGP-4 met the bar for Draft Standard through real implementations and real networks.

tldr.problem: To advance a routing protocol to Draft Standard, the IAB and IESG required documentation that the protocol satisfied the general and Draft Standard requirements of the routing protocol standardization criteria.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reports on BGP-4 implementations, production use, MIB, security, the move to classless routing, and open issues with metrics, internal peering and route dynamics.
tldr.outcome: It records several independent interoperable implementations and BGP-4 use between all significant autonomous systems at the time, and it flags work still needed.

today: RFC 1773 is an Informational report from March 1995 that obsoletes RFC 1656. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; its observations describe BGP-4 as it stood at the time of writing.

sections.title: Purpose of the Report
sections.content:
RFC 1773 documents how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard were satisfied by Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4). It is the second of two reports on BGP. As required by the IAB and IESG, the first report presents a performance analysis.

The sections that follow show how BGP meets the General Requirements in Section 3.0 and the Requirements for Draft Standard in Section 5.0 of RFC 1264, the Internet Routing Protocol Standardization Criteria. The report builds on early work by Peter Lothberg, Andrew Partan and others, presented at the Twenty-fifth IETF meeting.
sections.eli5: Before a rule can be called grown up, someone has to show it works in practice. This memo is that proof for a routing protocol.

sections.title: From BGP Version 1 to Version 4
sections.content:
BGP is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol designed for TCP/IP internets. Version 1 was published in RFC 1105, and versions 2, 3 and 4 followed. All functionality of the earlier versions is present in version 4.

Version 2 removed the "up", "down" and "horizontal" relations between autonomous systems and introduced path attributes. Version 3 lifted some limits on the NEXT_HOP attribute and added the BGP Identifier field to the OPEN message. Version 4 replaced class-based reachability with prefixes of arbitrary length, let AS-PATH describe sets of autonomous systems, renamed the INTER-AS metric as the MULTI-EXIT-DISCRIMINATOR, and added LOCAL-PREFERENCE and AGGREGATOR.

A BGP-4 Management Information Base has been published. Apart from a few system variables, it has two tables: the BGP Peer Table, with state and activity of peer connections, and the BGP Received Path Attribute Table, with all attributes received from all peers before local routing policy is applied.
sections.eli5: BGP got better in steps, like a game that gets new rules each year. The biggest change in version 4 lets one note describe a whole group of networks instead of just one.

sections.title: Implementations and Operational Experience
sections.content:
The memo lists five independent implementations in the operational Internet: cisco Systems, the gated consortium, 3COM, Bay Networks (Wellfleet) and Proteon. It notes that BGP-4 proved relatively simple to implement, taking on average about 2 man/months of effort, not counting restructuring needed for CIDR. This satisfies the IAB/IESG demand for multiple interoperable, completely independent implementations.

BGP has been in production use since 1989 and BGP-4 since 1993. Links ranged from 28 Kbits/sec to 150 Mbits/sec, and the topologies from a sparse spanning tree to the dense NSFNET backbone. BGP-4 was used between all significant autonomous systems, including Alternet, ANS, Ebone, ICM, IIJ, MCI, NSFNET and Sprint. The largest backbone had nearly 90 BGP speakers, there were several hundred known BGP speaking routers, and the exterior routes carried were well over 20,000 aggregate entries.

Measurements at the interconnection points between CA*Net and the T1 NSFNET Backbone showed that BGP consumed clearly less bandwidth and CPU than EGP.
sections.eli5: Many different companies built their own versions and they all talked to each other. That is how you know a rule really works.

sections.title: Migrating to BGP-4
sections.content:
Some IETF members worried about moving from classful to classless protocols. The memo says BGP-4 was rushed into production because of the exponential growth of routing tables and the CPU and memory they required, so migration issues were set aside in favor of pragmatic deployment.

Proposed "route exploders", which would list the individual class-based networks of a CIDR allocation for BGP-3 routers, were rejected because they would hasten the need for more CPU and memory. The path most operators chose was called "CIDR, default, or die!".

Testing used a virtual "shadow" Internet linking Alternet, Ebone, ICM and cisco over GRE based tunnels, with BGP version 3 connections to production networks. BGP-4 routers negotiated BGP-4 with each other and spoke BGP-3 to others. Once satisfied, some sites withdrew their class-based advertisements and kept only CIDR aggregates, which pushed other transit providers to migrate, accept a default route, or lose connectivity to popular destinations.
sections.eli5: Everyone had to switch to a new way of writing addresses. A test network let them practice first, and then the early adopters nudged everyone else to follow.

sections.title: Open Issues: Metrics, Internal Peering and Dynamics
sections.content:
The MULTI-EXIT-DISCRIMINATOR (MED) is used when choosing among paths from different external peers in the same AS. It was purposely made a weak metric used late in best-path selection, so that peers could not shed or absorb traffic for networks they advertise. LOCAL-PREFERENCE lets an operator override the standard best-path choice without configuring each router. The memo calls out a shortcoming: the BGP-4 specification suggested no common default for LOCAL-PREF, which would help multi-vendor routers in one AS.

Another open area is a way for an originating AS to influence path selection when its transit providers connect to a third provider. One suggestion is an optional vector parallel to the AS-PATH where each transit AS gives a preference value.

In a large AS, internal BGP needs an n^2 mesh of TCP connections. BGP does not say how to propagate this information, and alternatives such as injecting attributes into the IGP, internal route reflectors or reliable multicast transport were under discussion. Finally, the memo says damping techniques, described in the appendix of RFC 1771, should be considered for mandatory inclusion in future BGP-like protocols.
sections.eli5: The report also lists things still on the to-do list, like how a small network can say which of its two roads it prefers, and how to stop big networks from needing a phone line to everyone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo states that BGP provides a flexible and extendible mechanism for authentication and security. All sessions are authenticated based on the BGP Identifier and the autonomous system number of a peer, and the protocol can carry an encrypted digital signature in every message. Authentication failures result in NOTIFICATION messages and immediate termination of the connection.

Because BGP runs over TCP and IP, any authentication or security mechanism of either can be added, but BGP is also vulnerable to the same denial of service or authentication attacks as any other TCP based protocol.
sections.eli5: Routers check who they are talking to and hang up if something looks wrong. But since they talk over the ordinary internet, they can still be bothered the same way anything else can.
